title: Dermot Morgan

{{Short description|Irish comedian and actor (1952–1998)}} {{EngvarB|date=August 2014}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2026}} {{Infobox person | name = Dermot Morgan | image = Dermot Morgan February 1993 In Dublin magazine.jpg | caption = Morgan in 1993 | birth_name = Dermot John Morgan | birth_date = {{Birth date|df=yes|1952|3|31}} | birth_place = [[Dublin]], Ireland | death_date = {{Death date and age|df=yes|1998|2|28|1952|3|31}} | death_place = [[Richmond, London]], England | resting_place= [[Deans Grange Cemetery]] | years_active = 1979–1998 | spouse = Susanne Garmatz | partner = Fiona Clarke | children = 3 | occupation = {{hlist|Comedian|actor}} }} '''Dermot John Morgan''' (31 March 1952 – 28 February 1998) was an Irish comedian and actor, best known for his role as the [[Father Ted Crilly|title character]] on the [[Channel 4]] sitcom ''[[Father Ted]]''. Morgan died one day after filming of the [[List of Father Ted episodes#Series 3 (1998)|third and final series]] of ''Father Ted'' was completed. In 1999 he was posthumously awarded the [[British Academy Television Award for Best Comedy Performance]]. ==Early life== Dermot John Morgan was born on 31 March 1952 in Dublin, the son of Donnchadh Morgan, a civil servant, gifted amateur artist and sculptor, and Hilda "Holly" (née Stokes). His father died young of an [[aneurysm]], leaving Holly with three children: Dermot, Paul, and Denise. A fourth child, Ruth, died in childhood in 1956.{{cite web|url=http://www.turtlebunbury.com/history/history_family/hist_family_morgan.html|title=A History of the Morgan Family - Father Ted's Forebears |publisher=turtlebunbury.com|last=Bunbury|first=Turtle|access-date=8 July 2015}} Morgan was educated at [[Oatlands College]] in Stillorgan and [[University College Dublin]], where he studied English literature and philosophy. During his time there, he honed his comic skills; he also fronted a country and Irish band named Big Gom and the Imbeciles, a kind of "tribute" act to [[Big Tom and The Mainliners]], a major Irish band of the era. According to Morgan in a January 1986 article, "Everybody slagged [[Country and Irish|country and western]] at some stage". Big Gom and the Imbeciles were never signed by a record label, and Morgan subsequently worked as a teacher, which, he admitted, was a type of performance in itself:
There is a comparison between the performance of a schoolteacher and performance in general. You're on your feet and you have to be able to think. The best way of maintaining discipline is to have the ready reply. That's what being a performer is like. If you have a rowdy crowd in a pub or cabaret somewhere you've got to be on top.
==Career== ===Father Trendy and ''The Live Mike''=== Morgan made his debut in the media on the ''[[Morning Ireland]]'' radio show produced by Gene Martin, whose sister Ella was the mother of one of Morgan's friends. It was through this contact that Morgan made the break into radio and eventually television. According to a 1986 article in the ''[[The Herald (Ireland)|Evening Herald]]'', Morgan first got nationwide attention through letters he sent in to the [[Mike Murphy (presenter)|Mike Murphy]] radio show:
"The letters were on anything, from sitting in the traffic to [[Moss Keane]]. Michael was quite biting in his humour at the time so my letters fitted in quite well with the show." And it was Mike Murphy who eventually gave him a regular spot on his TV series, ''[[The Live Mike]]''. Dermot had been asked to do a routine on a TV pilot show hosted by [[Brendan Balfe]]. That was when he first introduced his ever-so laid back character, Father Trendy. "After all the letters to him, and after Murph saw the pilot show, he asked me to come on his own show..."
Morgan subsequently came to prominence as part of ''The Live Mike'', which became hugely successful in Ireland. Between 1979 and 1982, Morgan played a range of comic characters who appeared between segments of the show. Morgan lampooned the rampant [[Modernism in the Catholic Church|Modernism]] within the Post–[[Vatican II]] [[Roman Catholic Church in Ireland]] by incorporating his Father Trendy character, a wishy-washy, trying-to-be-cool [[hippie]]-priest (modelled after Father [[Brian D'Arcy]]). Father Trendy always wore an [[Elvis Presley]]-style haircut and sometimes a [[leather jacket]]. He was also given to drawing ludicrous parallels between religion and secularism in two-minute 'sermons' to the camera. Morgan also satirised [[extreme nationalist]] "[[West Brit#Antonyms|Little Irelanders]]", by playing an irate and bigoted [[Gaelic Athletic Association|GAA]] member who waved his [[Hurley (stick)|hurley]] around while verbally attacking his pet hates. At the height of [[the Troubles]], Morgan also lampooned both [[the Wolfe Tones]] and the clichés of [[Irish rebel song]]s, which he said "always have lots of blood and guts and fire and thunder in them". He then sang his own parody of [[Thomas Davis (Young Irelander)|Thomas Osborne Davis]]'s iconic song "[[A Nation Once Again]]", about the martyrdom of Fido, a dog who saves his [[Irish Republican Army|IRA]] master by eating a [[hand grenade]] during a search of the house by the [[Black and Tans]] during the [[Irish War of Independence]]. When Fido [[fart]]s and the grenade accidentally detonates, the Black and Tans comment, "'Scuse me mate, was that something your dog ate?" The song climaxed with the words: "I hope that I shall live to see Fido an Alsatian once again." [https://madmusic.com/song_details.aspx?SongID=41477 An Alsatian Once Again] ===As a singer: "Thank You Very Much, Mr. Eastwood"=== Morgan released a comedy single, "Thank You Very Much, Mr. Eastwood", in December 1985 on [[Dolphin Records (Ireland)|Dolphin Records]].{{cite news|first=Anthony|last=Hayward|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/obituary-dermot-morgan-1147951.html|title=Obituary: Dermot Morgan|newspaper=[[The Independent]]|date=2 March 1998|access-date=19 July 2010}} It was a take on the fawning praise that internationally successful Irish boxer [[Barry McGuigan]] gave his manager, Barney Eastwood, at the end of successive bouts. The single 'featured' impressions of McGuigan, [[Ronald Reagan]], [[Bob Geldof]] and [[Pope John Paul II]],New Island Books, 1998. and was the [[List of Irish Singles Chart Christmas number ones|Christmas number one]] in the [[Irish Singles Chart]] for 1985.{{cite web|url=https://www.irma.ie/christmas-number-ones/|title=The Irish Charts - All there is to know|work=irishcharts.ie}}{{Cite web |last=Curran |first=Aidan |date=23 February 2022 |title=Dermot Morgan – 'Thank You Very Much Mr Eastwood' |url=https://irishnumberones.com/2022/02/23/dermot-morgan-thank-you-very-much-mr-eastwood/ |access-date=25 November 2024 |website=Irish Number Ones |language=en}} Morgan spoke later to the press that he was "a bit worried" that his "take off" of the Pope during the song could have been received badly by the public, especially in [[Northern Ireland]] due to [[The Troubles|tensions there]] at the time.{{Cite news |last= Bradley | first= Dominic | date=15 December 1985 |title= Mr. Eastwood... Eh... Thank You |newspaper= Sunday News |language=en|page=29 }} [[Barry Devlin]], the former [[Horslips]] lead singer produced the single,{{Cite news |last= Boland | first= John | date=24 December 1985 |title= Modest Morgan |newspaper= [[Evening Press]] |language=en|page=16 }} whilst [[Paul McGuinness]], the [[U2]] manager, "struck a deal" for its release in Britain, with Morgan clarifying "I don't think he particularly wants to get involved with comedians. I think he just liked the idea and looked after some of the business for me." Speaking with the ''[[The Herald (Ireland)|Evening Herald]]'' in January 1986, Morgan announced that he would shortly be filming an accompanying [[music video]] for the single at [[Windmill Lane Studios|Windmill Lane Film Studios]] in Dublin:
But the fun doesn't stop there. In fact, ''Thank You Very Much, Mr. Eastwood'' is just the first part of a new major offensive by Mr. Morgan on the Irish comedy scene... "I'm going to be doing an album next as the interest is now there and I have plenty of original material lying around. The video for the single is also part of a 20 minute pilot programme that myself and Windmill Lane studios are putting together. It's a full comedy production and we hope to interest [[RTÉ]] and [[Channel 4]] with it." Dermot wants to get a comedy series off the ground made by an independent film company and he hopes to sell it both here and in Britain.{{Cite news |last= Russell | first= Paul | date=1986-01-04 |title= Dermot Morgan Says Thank You |newspaper= [[The Herald (Ireland)|Evening Herald]]|language=en|page=16 }}
===''Scrap Saturday''=== Morgan's biggest Irish broadcasting success occurred in the late 1980s on the Saturday morning radio comedy show ''[[Scrap Saturday]]'', in which Morgan, co-scriptwriter [[Gerard Stembridge]], [[Owen Roe (actor)|Owen Roe]] and [[Pauline McLynn]] mocked Ireland's political, business and media establishment. The show's treatment of the relationship between the ever-controversial [[Taoiseach]] [[Charles Haughey]] and his press secretary [[P. J. Mara]] proved particularly popular, with Haughey's dismissive attitude towards Mara and the latter's adoring and grovelling attitude towards his boss winning critical praise. Morgan pilloried Haughey's propensity for claiming a family connection to almost every part of Ireland he visited by referring to a famous advertisement for [[Harp Lager]], which played on the image of someone returning home and seeking friends. The Haughey/Mara "double act" became the star turn in a series that mocked both sides of the political divide, from Haughey and his advisors to opposition [[Fine Gael]] TD [[Michael Noonan (Fine Gael politician)|Michael Noonan]] as [[Limerick]] disk jockey "Morning Noon'an Night". When RTÉ axed the show in the early 1990s a national outcry ensued. Morgan lashed the decision, calling it "a shameless act of broadcasting cowardice and political subservience".{{citation needed|date=January 2015}} An RTÉ spokesman said: "The show is not being axed. It's just not being continued!"{{citation needed|date=January 2015}} In 1991, Morgan received a [[Jacob's Awards|Jacob's Award]] for his contribution to ''Scrap Saturday'' from the Irish national newspaper radio critics. ===''Father Ted''=== Already a celebrity in Ireland, Morgan got his big break in Britain with [[Channel 4]]'s Irish sitcom ''[[Father Ted]]'', which ran for three series from 1995 to 1998. Writers [[Graham Linehan]] and [[Arthur Mathews (writer)|Arthur Mathews]] auditioned many actors for the title role, but Morgan's enthusiasm won him the part. ''Father Ted'' focuses on the misadventures of three morally dubious Irish Catholic priests, whose transgressions have caused them to be exiled to the fictional Craggy Island, off the west coast of Ireland. ====BAFTA Award==== In 1996, ''Father Ted'' won a [[British Academy of Film and Television Arts|BAFTA]] award for [[British Academy Television Award for Best Comedy (Programme or Series)|Best Comedy Series]]. The same year Morgan also won a [[National Comedy Awards|British Comedy Award]] for Top TV Comedy Actor, and McLynn was awarded Top TV Comedy Actress. In 1999, ''Father Ted'' won a second BAFTA for Best Comedy, with Morgan being awarded [[British Academy Television Award for Best Comedy Performance|Best Comedy Performance]] posthumously. ===Unreleased works=== Morgan said in an interview with [[Gay Byrne]] on ''The Late Late Show'' in 1996 that he was writing a screenplay titled ''Miracle of the Magyars'', based on a real-life incident in the 1950s when the [[Archbishop of Dublin (Catholic Church)|Archbishop of Dublin]] [[John Charles McQuaid]] forbade Catholics from attending a football match between the [[Ireland national football team (FAI)|Republic of Ireland]] and [[Yugoslavia national football team|Yugoslavia]] on religious and spiritual grounds. Yugoslavia won the match 4–1. Morgan planned to use Hungary as the opposing side to the Republic of Ireland – hence the title. At the time of his death in 1998, he had completed the screenplay but the film was never made. Morgan's first project after ''Father Ted'' was to be ''Re-united'', a sitcom about two retired footballers sharing a flat in London. According to former manager John Fisher, Morgan was writing the script for the programme and planned to take the part of "an [[Eamon Dunphy]]-type who had gone on to work in journalism, but had ended up living with an old football pal". [[Mel Smith]] was in talks for the role of the friend.{{cite web|url=http://www.herald.ie/entertainment/around-town/mel-and-dermot-had-show-lined-up-29442263.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131231002414/http://www.herald.ie/entertainment/around-town/mel-and-dermot-had-show-lined-up-29442263.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=31 December 2013|title=Mel and Dermot had show lined up|work=herald.ie|last=Sweeney|first=Ken|date=23 July 2013|access-date=26 July 2013}} Morgan had been commissioned to write a drama series for the BBC.{{cite web|url=http://www.independent.ie/lifestyle/the-day-the-laughter-died-26450746.html|title=The day the laughter died|last=Egan|first=Barry|work=[[Irish Independent]]|date=1 June 2008|access-date=6 August 2015 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170709034836/https://www.independent.ie/lifestyle/the-day-the-laughter-died-26450746.html | archive-date = 9 July 2017}} ==Personal life== Morgan was married to Susanne Garmatz, a German woman, with whom he had two sons.{{cite news|url=http://www.independent.ie/entertainment/tv-radio/my-dad-was-fr-ted-and-i-still-miss-him-terribly-1661572.html|title=My dad was Fr Ted (and I still miss him terribly)|newspaper=Irish Independent |date=5 March 2009 |access-date=5 March 2009}} He later began a relationship with Fiona Clarke, with whom he had another son. Although he had been raised as a Catholic and had briefly considered becoming a priest during childhood, Morgan became an [[Atheism|atheist]] in his later life, and he was critical of the Catholic Church."Craggy Island would soak up the irony. From beyond the grave, Dermot Morgan, a staunch atheist who savaged the Catholic Church, is delivering a final kick to the priests who gave him a hero's send-off." Rory Carroll, 'Catholic critic Father Ted still causing controversy', ''The Guardian'', 23 April 1998, Pg. 4.{{cite web|url=http://spiritofgenovia.com/frted/d_morgan/obit_1.htm|title=Father Ted is dead|website=spiritofgenovia.com|access-date=2 May 2019|archive-date=3 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303212227/http://spiritofgenovia.com/frted/d_morgan/obit_1.htm|url-status=dead}} He supported Irish football clubs [[Shamrock Rovers F.C.]]{{cite news |title=Rovers Supporters Boycott Tolka |url=https://www.rte.ie/archives/2017/0813/896014-shamrock-rovers-on-the-move/ |access-date=1 February 2025 |publisher=RTE Sports}} and [[University College Dublin A.F.C.|UCD]], as well as English football club [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]]. ==Death== [[File:Dermot Morgan Memorial Chair.jpg|thumb|right|upright|The "Joker's Chair", a memorial to Morgan in Merrion Square, Dublin]] [[File:Dermot Morgan Grave.jpg|thumb|Morgan's grave in [[Dean's Grange Cemetery]], south County Dublin]] Before location filming on the third and final series of ''Father Ted'', Morgan underwent a mandatory medical examination in which he was found to have [[hypertension]], and was prescribed medication.{{Cite web|url=http://www.irishmirror.ie/whats-on/film-and-tv/tragic-dermot-morgan-under-serious-2962555|title=Tragic Dermot Morgan was under serious stress when he died aged 45 says Fr Ted star Frank Kelly|last=De-Burca|first=Demelza|date=27 December 2013|website=irishmirror|access-date=1 December 2019}} On 28 February 1998, one day after recording [[Going to America|the series' final episode]], Morgan suffered a heart attack while hosting a dinner party at his home in London's [[St Margarets, London|St Margarets]] area, at which the Scottish musician [[Jim Diamond (singer)|Jim Diamond]] was present. Guests and paramedics tried to revive him at his home. He was rushed to [[West Middlesex University Hospital]] in [[Isleworth]], but despite further resuscitation efforts, he died.{{cite news |title='Father Ted' dies. Irish TV Star collapses at party |publisher=The Richmond & Twickenham Informer |date=6 March 1998 |page=5}} He was 45 years old.{{cite news | url = https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/ireland-mourns-comic-talent-as-father-ted-actor-dies-aged-45-1147870.html | title = Ireland mourns comic talent as 'Father Ted' actor dies, aged 45 | last = Murdoch | first = Alan | date = 2 March 1998 | website = [[The Independent]] | access-date = 26 February 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201112023127/http://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/ireland-mourns-comic-talent-as-father-ted-actor-dies-aged-45-1147870.html | archive-date = 12 November 2020}} Morgan's sister Denise said, "He wasn't feeling great at the end of the meal and I went to the bedroom with him. He had a heart attack, and I didn't recognise it. From my limited training in first aid, I wasn't sure exactly what was happening. The symptoms didn't match what the books said. I said to him 'I think you are okay' and we went back to the table. He apologised for having left the room and the next thing he just collapsed. We tried to resuscitate him but it didn't work."{{cite web|url=http://www.thefreelibrary.com/MY+BROTHER+SAID+SORRY,+AND+THEN+HE+COLLAPSED%3B+IT+WAS+A+LONG+ROAD+TO...-a0101554135|title=MY BROTHER SAID SORRY, AND THEN HE COLLAPSED; IT WAS A LONG ROAD TO FAME FOR DERMOT MORGAN.. BUT SUCCESS WAS CUT SHORT BY HUGE HEART ATTACK. – Free Online Library|access-date=8 April 2014}} ''Father Ted'' co-star [[Frank Kelly]] said, "Dermot's mind was mercurial. I think he was a kind of comedic meteor. He burned himself out."{{cite web |last1=MacMillan |first1=Jane |title=Father Ted star Dermot Morgan dies |url=http://spiritofgenovia.com/frted/d_morgan/morgan_obit_teleg1.html |website=Electronic Telegraph |access-date=2 November 2019 |date=2 March 1998 |archive-date=9 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160409091400/http://spiritofgenovia.com/frted/d_morgan/morgan_obit_teleg1.html |url-status=dead }} Despite Morgan's atheism, a Catholic requiem mass was offered for him at St Therese's Church in the [[South Dublin]] suburb of [[Mount Merrion]]. The mass was attended by Irish President [[Mary McAleese]], her predecessor [[Mary Robinson]], and many of the Irish political and religious leaders who had been the targets of his satire in ''Scrap Saturday''. His body was cremated at [[Glasnevin Cemetery]], and his ashes were buried in the family plot at [[Dean's Grange Cemetery]].[http://www.dmtribute.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk/ "Dermot Morgan Tribute"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061217124119/http://www.dmtribute.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk/ |date=17 December 2006 }}. dmtribute.pwp.blueyonder.co.uk. Retrieved March 2011. ==Legacy== "The Joker's Chair", a bronze throne by sculptor Catherine Green, was unveiled by then-Taoiseach Bertie Ahern in [[Merrion Square]], Dublin. It bears his name, date of birth, and date of death. In December 2013, the documentary ''Dermot Morgan – Fearless Funnyman'' aired on [[RTÉ One]].{{cite web|url = http://www.rte.ie/presspack/2013/12/27/dermot-morgan-fearless-funnyman/|title=DERMOT MORGAN – FEARLESS FUNNYMAN|date=27 December 2013|work=RTÉ |access-date=2 January 2014}} A plaque outside McGuire's shop in [[Mount Merrion]] was unveiled in 2016. A wax statue of Morgan stands in the national wax museum in Dublin as part of a "Father Ted's Room" display.{{cite web|url=https://waxmuseumplus.ie/attractions/father-teds-room/|work=[[National Wax Museum Plus]]|title=Father Ted's room|date=18 March 2020|access-date=5 December 2021}} ==Appearances== ===Television=== *''[[The Live Mike]]'' (1979–1982) *''[[Father Ted]]'' (1995–1998) *''[[Have I Got News for You]]'' (1996–97; episodes 11.02 and 14.03) *''[[Shooting Stars (British TV series)|Shooting Stars]]'' (1 episode, 1996) *''[[That's Showbusiness]]'' (1 episode, 1996) ===Radio=== *''[[Scrap Saturday]]'' (1989–1991) ===Film=== *''[[Taffin]]'' (1988) *''[[The First Snow of Winter]]'' (1998, voice in UK version) ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} ==External links== * {{IMDb name|0604607}} {{British Academy Television Award for Best Comedy Performance}} {{RTÉ Radio 1}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Morgan, Dermot}} [[Category:1952 births]] [[Category:1998 deaths]] [[Category:20th-century Irish male actors]] [[Category:Alumni of University College Dublin]] [[Category:Best Comedy Performance BAFTA Award (television) winners]] [[Category:Burials at Deans Grange Cemetery]] [[Category:Critics of the Catholic Church]] [[Category:Former Roman Catholics]] [[Category:Irish atheists]] [[Category:Irish comedy musicians]] [[Category:Irish former Christians]] [[Category:Irish impressionists (entertainers)]] [[Category:Irish male comedians]] [[Category:Irish male television actors]] [[Category:Irish parodists]] [[Category:Parody musicians]] [[Category:Irish satirical musicians]] [[Category:Irish schoolteachers]] [[Category:Irish sketch comedians]] [[Category:Irish expatriates in England]] [[Category:Jacob's Award winners]] [[Category:People educated at Oatlands College]] [[Category:Radio personalities from the Republic of Ireland]] [[Category:People from Stillorgan]] [[Category:Broadcasters from County Dublin]] [[Category:1970s in Irish comedy]] [[Category:1980s in Irish comedy]] [[Category:1990s in Irish comedy]]
